I’m 56, been farming this land in Quzhou since I was a boy. I never went to school, but I know every inch of my fields and every turn of the seasons. The North China Plain gives us two crops a year if you work fast, and I’ve always done the winter wheat–summer maize rotation. It’s what the soil knows, what the market wants, and what puts food on the table.

This year I’ll stick to that. I have 4 mu of good flat land. In October I’ll sow winter wheat—an improved variety that the county ag station recommends, not the old seed my grandfather used. It stands up better to the dry spring winds. I’ll plough and rotary till before sowing to break up the corn stubble. I’ll put down about 22 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus 7 kg each of phosphorus and potassium. The wheat needs three irrigations: one before winter to help it survive the cold, one at jointing when the stems shoot up, and one at heading so the grains fill properly. I’ll spray pesticides twice, once for aphids and once for rust if the weather turns damp. I expect around 550 kg per mu if the spring drought doesn’t bite too hard.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I’ll plant hybrid summer maize. There’s barely a day to waste. I’ll rotary till again, broadcast about 20 kg nitrogen per mu, 6 kg phosphorus, and 6 kg potassium. Maize drinks water at silking, so I’ll irrigate twice—once right after sowing if June is dry, and once at the big ear stage. Two pesticide sprays should handle the corn borers. If the autumn rains hold off long enough for harvest, I should get 650 kg per mu.

That’s my plan. It’s not fancy, but it’s honest, and it’s kept my family going for decades.
